title: Lecture on consistent hashing, one speaker, a 20 second silent gap mid-way

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: Today's lecture is about a problem that sounds trivial and isn't: how do you decide which machine in a cluster should store a particular piece of data? We'll start with the naive answer, show why it fails, and build up to consistent hashing, which was introduced by David Karger and colleagues at MIT in 1997. By the end you should be able to explain what a virtual node is, why the ring has 2 to the power of 32 positions, and what happens to your cache hit rate when a server dies at three in the morning.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: The naive answer is modulo hashing. Take the key, hash it with something like SHA-256, interpret the result as a big integer, and compute the remainder when you divide by the number of servers, N. If you have five servers, key number 42 might land on server 3. This is fast, it is stateless, and every client that knows N and the hash function agrees on the answer without talking to anyone. Lookup is O(1). For a fixed cluster, it is nearly perfect.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: The trouble starts when N changes. Suppose you go from five servers to six. A key stays on its server only if its hash gives the same remainder modulo five and modulo six, which happens for roughly one key in six. So about 83 percent of your keys move. For a cache, that means a sudden miss rate of 83 percent, and every one of those misses falls through to your database, which was sized for a cache hit rate above 95 percent. Engineers call this a thundering herd, and it has taken down more than one production system.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: Consistent hashing fixes this by changing what the hash is mapped onto. Instead of dividing by N, imagine a circle, a ring, with positions numbered from 0 to 2 to the power of 32 minus 1. Hash each server's name onto the ring. Hash each key onto the same ring. To find the server for a key, start at the key's position and walk clockwise until you meet the first server. That server owns the key.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: Let me make that concrete with small numbers. Suppose the ring has 100 positions, and servers A, B and C sit at positions 10, 40 and 80. A key hashing to 25 walks clockwise and meets B at 40. A key hashing to 85 walks past 100, wraps around to zero, and meets A at 10. Now add server D at position 60. Only keys between 40 and 60 change owner, moving from C to D. A key at 25 is still on B, a key at 85 is still on A. Twenty positions out of 100 moved, which is the share D now owns, and nothing else was touched.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: In general, adding a sixth server to a ring of five moves only the keys that the new server takes over. On average only one key in N moves, so going from five servers to six moves about 17 percent of the keys, not 83. Remove a server and the same logic applies in reverse: its keys fall to the next server clockwise, and nobody else is disturbed.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: There is a catch, and it is the reason the textbook version is rarely deployed as it is. With only five points on a ring, the gaps between them are uneven. One server might own 35 percent of the key space and another only 8. The load is then badly skewed, and when a server fails, all of its keys land on a single neighbour, which may double that neighbour's load and make it fail too. This is the cascade failure pattern.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: The solution is virtual nodes. Instead of placing each physical server on the ring once, place it many times, say 100 to 200 points, each derived by hashing the server name together with a replica number: server-A-0, server-A-1, and so on. With 150 virtual nodes per server, the law of large numbers works in your favour, and each server's share of the ring converges to within a few percent of one over N. When a server fails, its 150 ranges are scattered around the ring and are absorbed by many different neighbours, so no single machine takes the whole hit.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: Virtual nodes also give you a convenient dial. A machine with twice the memory can be given twice as many virtual nodes and therefore twice the share of the keys. Amazon's Dynamo paper, published in 2007, relied on exactly this idea to deal with heterogeneous hardware, and added replication: each key is stored not only on the first server clockwise, but on the next three distinct physical servers, so that a single failure loses no data.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: A word on a problem that hashing does not solve: hot keys. If a single key receives a thousand times the traffic of its neighbours, it does not matter how evenly you spread the key space, because one server will be overwhelmed. The standard remedies are to replicate hot keys to several servers and have clients pick one at random, or to put a small local cache in front of the cluster. Both are application-level decisions that sit on top of the hashing scheme, not inside it.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: What does this cost? Lookup is no longer a single division. You keep the virtual nodes in a sorted array and use binary search, so a lookup is O(log V), where V is the total number of virtual nodes. For 1,000 servers with 150 virtual nodes each, that is 150,000 entries and about 17 comparisons. That is still microseconds. Memory is a few megabytes. The real costs are operational: every client needs the same view of the ring, so membership changes have to be propagated, and during propagation two clients can briefly disagree about who owns a key.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: Consistent hashing is not the only approach. Rendezvous hashing, also called highest random weight hashing, was published in 1996 by Thaler and Ravishankar. For each key you compute a score for every server by hashing the key together with the server's name, and you pick the server with the highest score. There is no ring, no virtual nodes, and the balance is excellent, but a lookup costs O(N) hash computations, which matters at large N. For a few dozen servers it is often simpler and perfectly adequate.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: Google's Maglev load balancer, described in a 2016 paper, takes a third route. It builds a fixed-size lookup table, with a prime number of entries such as 65,537, filled in so that every backend gets an almost equal share of the entries. Lookup is a single array access, and when a backend changes, only a small fraction of entries change. The price is that building the table takes time, and the disruption on change is somewhat higher than with a ring.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: To summarise. Modulo hashing is simple but moves most of your data when the cluster changes. Consistent hashing moves roughly one over N of it, at the price of a sorted structure and some operational care. Virtual nodes smooth the load and spread failures. Rendezvous hashing trades lookup time for simplicity, and Maglev trades build time for lookup speed. When you are asked in an interview which one to use, the right first answer is: it depends on how often your membership changes and how many nodes you have. Thank you, and see you next week.
